title: Value Flows
one_liner: Use smooth continuous models to estimate the full shape of future rewards, then weight learning by how uncertain each estimate is.
lead: Most RL algorithms collapse future returns down to a single number, missing what the data actually looks like. This paper uses a flow-matching model (a tool for learning the full shape of possible outcomes, like tracing a smooth path from random noise to real data) to estimate all the different futures that might happen—and then uses that full picture to decide which transitions deserve the most learning effort.

problem.h2: Why flattening returns costs you information
paras: Today's RL algorithms treat future returns like a thermometer reading: they estimate one scalar number (expected return from this state). But in reality, futures are messy. From the same state, you might get reward 5 some days and reward 20 other days—the data is spread out. Old methods throw away that shape.

If you use one number to decide where to explore or whether an action is safe, you miss critical information. A state with returns [5, 5, 5] (reliable, always low) looks the same as [1, 10, 20] (highly uncertain). But they should receive different treatment: the uncertain one demands caution or extra learning.

callout.html: Learn a smooth curve (via flow-matching) that captures the full shape of possible returns, then use how spread-out that curve is to weight which transitions to learn hardest from.

panels.title: 1. Old way: collapse to one number
panels.caption: Each state boils down to one expected value. Shape is lost.

panels.title: 2. Reality: the spread matters
panels.caption: Real data: returns cluster but spread wide. Prediction must capture that.

panels.title: 3. Flow-matching: learn the shape
panels.caption: A neural network traces a continuous path from noise to realistic returns.

panels.title: 4. Compute variance from the curve
panels.caption: Wider spread means higher variance, so stronger learning weight for that transition.

panels.title: 5. Pay most attention to the uncertain ones
panels.caption: High-uncertainty transitions get the strongest training nudge. Safe ones train lightly.

steps.text: Gather (state, action, next state, reward) from the environment or stored data.
Train a vector field (a function that nudges random noise toward real returns) using flow-matching loss.
For each transition, compute how spread-out the learned distribution is (via the flow model's derivatives).
Scale the loss for each transition: high variance gets a big multiplier, low variance gets a small one.
Sample actions from the flow model or use deterministic action selection to exploit the learned return estimates.

paras: Instead of learning to predict a single scalar return, the paper trains a vector field (a learned function that maps random noise toward plausible returns). This vector field encodes the entire shape of possible future returns—capturing not just the average but also how spread out the possibilities are.

hidden.h2: Return variance: how spread-out is the future?
hidden.name: Return variance (width of the distribution)
paras: The hidden quantity is return variance: how far apart the possible future rewards tend to be. If a state has low variance, the returns cluster tight. If high variance, they scatter wide. This is computed directly from the learned flow model by taking its derivatives.

The paper estimates variance by linearizing the flow model's prediction and computing the noise sensitivity—essentially, how much a small change in the random input pushes the output around. High sensitivity means high variance.

heat.caption: Darker means higher return variance. Highlighted states get stronger learning weights.

reads.html: Variance is how spread-out the returns are. A wide spread means the future is unpredictable from this state.
The paper computes variance via a Taylor linearization of the return prediction around the noise input, then differentiates through the flow model.

mechanism.h2: Why focusing learning effort on high-variance states works
paras: When return variance is high, the model is most uncertain. Investing learning effort into uncertain transitions makes sense: a small error in a high-stakes prediction (wide spread, many possible futures) has bigger impact than the same error in a confident prediction (tight spread).

Flow-matching is well-suited to this task because it directly models the probability density (the shape of returns), unlike older methods that only predict a mean. The flow model's derivatives naturally give you variance. By reweighting the loss with variance, you steer learning updates toward states where better prediction matters most.

The mechanism also captures the exploring-vs-exploiting tradeoff: high-variance states are candidates for deeper exploration (because you have not seen enough examples to trust your estimate) or safer policies (because the actual returns might be much worse than the mean). Learning their returns accurately improves both safety and regret, because you are no longer blindly relying on the average.

stages.s: Transition: state, action, reward, next state
Flow model transforms noise into predicted return distribution
Compute variance of distribution via derivatives
Scale loss by variance weight: high variance gets big weight
Learning update: strong nudge where uncertainty is high

math.h2: The flow-matching loss and variance reweighting
math.words: Loss = sum over transitions of [ variance-weight(s,a) * flow-matching-error(s,a) ]
math.equation: L_Value = sum_i w(s_i, a_i) * ||v_theta(z_t | t, s_i, a_i) - (z_0 - z_1) / t||^2
symbols: confidence weight derived from return variance at (state, action)
the learned vector field (neural network) parameterized by theta
random noise at time step t, gradually denoised to a return
the actual return observed from data
terminal noise (start of the denoising path)
time parameter in the flow (0 = noise, 1 = real return)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose two transitions: T1 and T2, both predict return 15.
T1 has low variance (spread small): w(T1) = 0.2
T2 has high variance (spread wide): w(T2) = 1.0
Same prediction error, but T2 receives 5x stronger training nudge because its future is more uncertain.

math.note: The weight w prioritizes learning where the model is least confident; the flow-matching loss trains the vector field to trace the true return distribution.

bars.h2: Return distribution quality: old vs new

charts.title: Quantile-based method (old way)
charts.note: Quantile methods discretize the space and may miss smooth fine-grained structure.

charts.title: Value Flows (this paper)
charts.note: Continuous flow model captures the full shape; weighting by variance focuses learning on uncertain transitions.

items.html: If the initial vector field is bad, the denoising path may be erratic. Solution: use a pre-trained diffusion model or warm-start on auxiliary data.

If a transition is high-variance due to noise (not true uncertainty), reweighting amplifies the noise. Solution: smooth the variance estimates or use a confidence penalty on uncertain-but-rare transitions.

High variance might mean the model is ignorant (epistemic) or the world is truly random (aleatoric). The current method does not distinguish them. Solution: ensemble flow models or count visit frequency to flag rarely-seen states.

Combine variance reweighting with exploration bonuses (to handle epistemic uncertainty) and a smoothness prior on the learned flow (to avoid noise amplification). Validate on both state-based and image-based benchmarks across offline and online-to-online settings.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small offline RL environment (e.g., a simple navigation task with 5–10 states). Collect a dataset of trajectories. Train a flow-matching model to predict returns and compute variance for each transition. Then train a standard RL algorithm but with and without variance-based reweighting. Track both success rate on new episodes and the quality of return predictions (e.g., how accurately you predict the 90th percentile return).
demo.closing: The demo reveals the core principle: states with uncertain futures must receive stronger learning updates because a small prediction error in a high-uncertainty scenario compounds into bigger mistakes than the same error in a confident scenario, and a flow model's mathematical derivatives compute that uncertainty automatically by measuring how much the model's output wobbles when you perturb the input noise.
